text: Code that passes tests is necessary but not sufficient for a library someone else can actually use. This lesson writes quantumlib's documentation — docstrings following lesson four's standard, a README, and a worked example — closing the gap lesson twenty-one deliberately deferred from the requirements document.

This lesson covers writing complete docstrings for all three capstone modules, writing a README that documents validated backends and pinned SDK versions rather than just installation steps, building a worked example script a new user could run end to end, and documenting the capstone's own reproducibility setup as a model for users of the library.

Following lesson four's template, the GHZ-circuit docstring now states which qubit plays which role, what the expected measurement distribution looks like, and which backend and SDK version this was actually validated against. Notice the honest line stating it hasn't yet been validated against real hardware — lesson four argued documentation should state what's actually been checked, and overstating validation coverage here would be exactly the kind of undocumented claim that lesson warned against.

A worked example script builds a GHZ circuit, runs it on a seeded local simulator backend, and computes and prints the z-score against the expected fifty-fifty split along with the explicit confidence threshold used — not just pass or fail. A new user reading the output learns not just the verdict but the standard it was judged against, consistent with every statistical test built across Chapter 2.

As a model for users of the library, the reproducibility documentation should walk through exactly what the Chapter 4 lab demonstrated: tag an experiment, commit the lockfile, save an experiment record, and show the fire-drill reproduction steps — so anyone extending quantumlib with their own experiments has a template to follow rather than reinventing the practice from scratch.

Before considering the documentation complete: every public function documents circuit, qubit roles, expected distribution, and validated-against; the README states targeted SDKs and honest gaps rather than implying broader coverage; at least one runnable example script exists per module; and a reproducibility walkthrough exists modeling Chapters 4's practices. Next lesson closes the capstone and the course: a full code review against the requirements, and an honest accounting of what's done versus deferred.
